title: Listening: regional accents
goal: By the end of this lesson you can recognise the main features of Quebec pronunciation, tell apart some regional accents (Montreal, Quebec City, Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean, Gaspésie) from a European French accent, and keep understanding speakers whose accent is new to you.

body: Most Quebec speakers, from news anchors to teenagers, share a few features. Learn these first: they appear everywhere in the province.

1) *t* and *d* before *i* and *u* become 'ts' and 'dz': *tu dis* → 'tsu dzi', *mardi* → 'mar-dzi'. 2) *i*, *u* and *ou* become shorter and more open in closed syllables: *vite* sounds closer to English 'vit', *musique* to 'mu-zik'. 3) Long vowels, especially in stressed syllables, glide (diphthongs) in casual speech: *père* → 'paèr', *fête* → 'faèt', *neige* → 'naèj'.
learn.tip: Affrication (tsu, dzi) is standard Quebec pronunciation, not slang: you'll hear it on Radio-Canada.

body: Montreal French is urban and multilingual: you'll hear more English loanwords and code-switching, plus the accents of speakers whose first language is Arabic, Spanish, Haitian Creole, Vietnamese and more. Many older Montrealers roll their r with the tip of the tongue; most younger speakers use a throat (uvular) r.

Quebec City speakers use the uvular r, and their accent is often perceived by other Quebecers as a bit more measured. In practice the differences between Montreal and Quebec City are small compared to the regions: vocabulary and rhythm vary more than sounds.

Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean is famous for a strong, sing-song accent with long, rich diphthongs and a slower rhythm. People from the region are affectionately called *les Bleuets*, after the local wild blueberries.

Gaspésie is varied. Many speakers have a calm, slower rhythm and older rural vocabulary. Along the Baie-des-Chaleurs, the Acadian influence is audible: you may hear forms like *j'avons* (for *nous avons*) among older speakers. The Îles-de-la-Madeleine have their own Acadian-influenced accent.

A Paris accent has no 'ts/dz' (*tu dis* stays 'tu di'), no diphthongs, shorter vowels overall, and usually merges sounds Quebec keeps apart (*patte/pâte*, *brin/brun*). Intonation tends to rise at the end of each word group.

Southern France sounds different again: the final *-e* is often pronounced (*la vie-e*), and nasal vowels can end in a slight 'ng' (*pain* → 'peng'). Belgian and Swiss French have their own rhythms and words (*septante*, *nonante*).

Listen to the same content in different accents: a news bulletin from Radio-Canada, then a regional radio station, then a podcast from France. Focus on one feature at a time (affrication this lesson, diphthongs next week).
When you don't understand someone, ask politely: *Pardon, pouvez-vous répéter un peu plus lentement?* or *Excusez-moi, je n'ai pas bien saisi.* Most people are happy to slow down for a learner.

examples.en: You're saying you got here Tuesday?

examples.note: frette = froid, informal Quebec; à matin = ce matin

examples.fr: On va fêter ça avec mon père.
examples.en: We're going to celebrate with my dad.

examples.note: short, open i and u in closed syllables: 'muzik', 'vit'

examples.fr: J'ai mangé des pâtes, pas de la patte!
examples.note: Quebec keeps â and a distinct

examples.fr: Les Bleuets sont fiers de leur région.
examples.en: People from Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean are proud of their region.

examples.fr: En Gaspésie, on prend le temps de jaser.
examples.en: In Gaspésie, people take the time to chat.

examples.fr: À Paris, on dit « tu dis » sans le petit « s ».
examples.en: In Paris, they say 'tu dis' without the little 's'.
Sorry, could you repeat more slowly?

examples.fr: Je n'ai pas bien saisi ce que vous avez dit.
examples.en: I didn't quite catch what you said.

examples.fr: Elle a un petit accent de la Beauce.
examples.en: She has a slight Beauce accent.
examples.note: un petit accent = a slight accent
the rolled r of older Montrealers

examples.fr: En Belgique, on dit « septante » pour soixante-dix.
examples.en: In Belgium, they say 'septante' for seventy.

quebec.intro: Quebec pronunciation has features that change how familiar words sound. Here they are side by side with the 'textbook' pronunciation. Affrication (tsu, dzi) is standard Quebec; the other forms are casual.

items.note: t/d → ts/dz before i and u: standard Quebec pronunciation
moé and itou: informal, more common in the regions
a = elle, short open i; informal
traditional Acadian form, heard among older speakers in parts of Gaspésie and the Îles

drills.q: Which feature is typical of a Paris accent?
options: patte and pâte sound the same
drills.why: Paris usually merges a and â.

drills.en: Sorry, can you repeat more slowly?

drills.q: Il fait ___ à matin! (cold, informal Quebec)

vocab.ex: On a jasé toute la soirée.

pron.tip: Quebec: tsu dzi, mar-dzi. France: tu di, mar-di.
Quebec: p'tsitt, with a short open i. France: p'tit.
Casual Quebec: paèr, faèt (glide). France: pèr, fèt.
Quebec: pâte is darker, like 'pawt'; patte is bright 'pat'.
Quebec keeps two nasals: brin (bright), brun (rounded).
Often 'peng', with a slight g at the end.

dialogue.fr: Salut! Toi, t'es d'où? J'entends un petit accent.
dialogue.en: Hi! Where are you from? I hear a slight accent.

dialogue.fr: Moé, j'viens d'Alma, au Lac-Saint-Jean. Une vraie Bleuet! Pis toi?
dialogue.en: Me, I'm from Alma, in Lac-Saint-Jean. A real Bleuet! And you?

dialogue.fr: Moi, je viens de Lyon. Au début, je ne comprenais pas « tsu dzis ». Je pensais que tout le monde était enrhumé!
dialogue.en: I'm from Lyon. At first, I didn't understand 'tsu dzis'. I thought everyone had a cold!

dialogue.fr: Ha! Pis l'accent de Montréal, tu le comprends?
dialogue.en: Ha! And the Montreal accent, do you understand it?

dialogue.fr: Oui, mais les Montréalais mettent de l'anglais partout. Toi, tu parles plus lentement.
dialogue.en: Yes, but Montrealers put English everywhere. You speak more slowly.

dialogue.fr: Plus lentement, pis plus joliment! Ma grand-mère de Gaspé dit encore « j'avons » et « astheure ».
dialogue.en: More slowly, and more nicely! My grandmother from Gaspé still says 'j'avons' and 'astheure'.

dialogue.fr: « J'avons »? On dirait du vieux français!
C'est l'influence acadienne. Finalement, peu importe l'accent, on finit toujours par se comprendre.
dialogue.en: It's the Acadian influence. In the end, no matter the accent, we always end up understanding each other.

questions.q: What does B's grandmother from Gaspé still say?

speak.prompt: Read the same sentence twice, first with Quebec affrication, then 'France style': 'Tu dis que tu pars mardi midi?'
speak.model: Quebec : tsu dzi kuh tsu par mar-dzi mi-dzi? / France : tu di kuh tu par mar-di mi-di?

speak.prompt: Describe your own accent in French and what's hard for you to pronounce.
speak.model: J'ai un accent anglais assez prononcé. J'ai de la difficulté avec le r et avec la différence entre « tu » et « tout ».

speak.prompt: Ask someone politely to repeat, in three different ways.
speak.model: Pardon? / Excusez-moi, pouvez-vous répéter plus lentement? / Désolé, je n'ai pas bien saisi.

speak.prompt: Compare two accents you've heard (Montreal, a region, or France) in three sentences.
speak.model: À Montréal, les gens parlent vite et mélangent souvent le français et l'anglais. Au Lac-Saint-Jean, l'accent est plus chantant et plus lent. En France, on ne dit pas « tsu », mais « tu ».

write.prompt: Write 7–9 sentences about your experience with accents in French: which ones you find easy or hard, a funny misunderstanding, and your strategy for understanding new accents.
write.model: Quand je suis arrivé à Montréal, je trouvais l'accent québécois très difficile. Mes professeurs parlaient un français international, mais dans la rue, j'entendais « tsu dzis » et « moé ». Une fois, une collègue de Chicoutimi m'a dit qu'il faisait « frette », et j'ai pensé qu'elle parlait de son frère! Maintenant, je comprends bien les Montréalais, mais les accents des régions restent un défi. Les films français, par contre, me semblent plus faciles parce que les gens articulent beaucoup. Ma stratégie, c'est d'écouter la radio régionale de Radio-Canada dix minutes par jour. Et quand je ne comprends pas, je demande poliment de répéter. Peu importe l'accent, les gens apprécient toujours l'effort.

quiz.q: Which feature is standard Quebec pronunciation, used even on the news?
options: tsu / dzi before i and u

quiz.q: Diphthongs like 'faète' for fête are typical of…
quiz.why: Long vowels glide in casual Quebec speech.

quiz.q: Which accent is described as strong and sing-song, with rich diphthongs?

quiz.why: Many Parisians merge the two nasals.

quiz.q: Which phrase asks someone to repeat?
Montreal French is especially marked by…
A rolled r with the tip of the tongue is mostly heard among…
quiz.why: Most younger speakers use a uvular r.
